<user_query>
take a look at the economic_tick_planning and @source/scenes/cards/organizing/organize_phase_tick.scene.dry files.  The idea here is that every month there is a calculation for the state of the economy.  An important part of this is that the power of the corporations to sway the electorate will be dependent on how profitable they are.

What are your initial impressions about the organization of this file?
</user_query>

Here are my first impressions, focusing on how the pieces are organized rather than whether the math is final.

## What’s working

**Spec vs. runtime split** — `economic_tick_planning` is a readable ledger of state (`trade_level`, corp/coop/drone cash, strength, markets) and flows (trade by phase → strength → spending → export/import/domestic). `organize_phase_tick.scene.dry` is the “install hooks on `Q`” scene. That’s a sensible pattern for Dendry: one visit defines `Q.monthly_tick_phase1`, something else calls it each month.

**Pipeline shape in the planning doc** — You’re thinking in the right order: exogenous trade → actor strength → spending → revenue buckets → redistribution. Corporate strength as the hinge for “how loud corps are in politics” fits your electorate goal; export revenue tied to strength and trade level is the right lever for profitability.

**Chunked functions in the tick file** — `trade_level_tick`, `tourism_revenue`, `longshore_revenue`, `corp_purchase`, `coop_purchase` map cleanly to sections in the planning doc. Easy to grow one sector at a time.

## Where organization gets muddy

**Three sources of truth** — The same economy lives in `economic_tick_planning`, `organize_phase_tick.scene.dry`, and a slice of `major/plan.txt`. Phase 2 trade growth in the planning file doesn’t match the multipliers in the tick scene (plan: grow `0.0005556`; code: shrink `0.9994444`). Without a single canonical doc or comments like `// see economic_tick_planning §Trade`, those will keep drifting.

**Planning file isn’t in the build** — No `.dry` extension, not referenced by scenes. Fine as a scratchpad, but it’s easy to treat it as “the spec” while only `.scene.dry` actually runs. I’d either rename/link it (`economic_tick_planning.md` + a one-line pointer in the tick scene) or fold the spec into comments at the top of `organize_phase_tick.scene.dry`.

**Bootstrap scene vs. monthly tick** — `organize_phase_tick` is `max-visits: 1` and only assigns `Q.monthly_tick_phase1`. The economy doesn’t run every month until something (likely `post_event` or `organize_phase_start` chain) calls that function. Right now that wiring isn’t visible in these two files, so “monthly economy” is organized as *library code on a card*, not as an obvious monthly pipeline. Worth making the call site explicit in the planning doc (“invoked from: post_event on-arrival”).

**Social vs. economic in one bag** — `organize_tick()` (protest / `non_violence`) sits beside `trade_level_tick()` and `economy_tick()`. Conceptually related, but different domains. Splitting into `social_tick()` vs `economy_tick()` (or two scenes / two JS blocks) would mirror your planning doc sections and keep electorate modifiers easier to trace.

**Incomplete orchestration** — `economy_tick()` only calls `trade_level()` (wrong name) and `corp_purchase()`; tourism, longshore, coop, and “check export revenues” from the plan aren’t in the pipeline yet. `monthly_tick_phase1` calls `econmy_tick()` (typo) instead of `economy_tick()`. So the *structure* says “orchestrator + sector functions,” but the orchestrator doesn’t match the plan’s checklist — easy to lose track of what’s implemented.

**Corp strength → electorate bridge isn’t in the file layout yet** — Planning centers `Corporate strength`; the tick file tracks `corp_money` / `corp_capital` but not `corp_strength`, and `post_event`’s `ElectorateModifier` catalog is story-stack-driven, not profit-driven. Organizationally, you’ll want one obvious path, e.g. `economy_tick` → `update_corp_strength()` → `Q.corp_electorate_pressure` → modifier row in `post_event`, or strength applied directly in `applyElectorateModifiers`.

## Smaller code-org signals (if you consolidate)

- Revenue helpers reference `Q.corp_tourism` / `Q.corp_longshore` while assigning `*_rev` — naming inconsistency will confuse maintenance.
- `corp_purchase` uses bare `corp_spend` / `corp_capital` instead of `Q.` — suggests this block was pasted mid-draft.
- `coop_purchase` stops at `Q.coop_spend` with no assignment — placeholder breaking the “one function, one responsibility” pattern.

## Summary

The **mental model is strong**: state list → phase-driven trade → strength/spending/revenue → political consequence. The **file organization is early-draft**: good separation of planning notes vs. tick implementation, but duplicated specs, a one-shot scene that doesn’t document its caller, and an orchestrator that doesn’t yet mirror the planning doc’s sections. For profitability → electorate, I’d make **corporate strength** (or a derived `corp_political_capital`) the explicit output of `economy_tick` and document that single variable as the handoff to `ElectorateModifier` in `post_event`.

If you want a next step, I can sketch a tightened layout (one checklist-ordered `economy_tick`, canonical variable names, and where to hook `monthly_tick_phase1` in the month loop) without implementing the full sim yet.

Added a **Polling & demographics** tab to `status.scene.dry`, modeled on the Weimar `@polls` block, using Mikasa’s five parties (Corp, Gang, Dems, Hate, Ind) and the same colors as the seat view.

### Structure (like `library.scene.dry`)
- **`@overview`** (default via `go-to: overview`) — seat projections (unchanged logic: Executive, Guilds, Districts D1–D7).
- **`@polls`** — popular-vote shares and per-stratum breakdown.
- Navigation choices stay **at the bottom** of each subscene (Dendry requirement).

### `@polls` content
1. **Projected election results** — executive-weighted popular vote %: `poll_exec_C`, `poll_exec_G`, etc., with tooltips.
2. **Detailed results by demographic** — one line per stratum (`rich`, `first`, `second`, `coop`, `drone`, `alien`, `deeper`) using `*_poll_*` variables.

### Data wiring (`root_new.scene.dry`)
`writePollDisplaysToQ()` runs inside `Q.update_projections()`:
- Totals executive-chamber votes across all voter blocks for national %.
- Aggregates by stratum for the demographic lines.

The overview still shows **seat counts** (`Exec_C`, `Docks_C`, …); polls show **vote share** — parallel to Weimar’s “% votes” vs your existing chamber math.

**Note:** If `dendrynexus` failed earlier, `npm install dendrynexus` was run to fix a corrupted `lib/cli/main.js` from the old shim. Build passes now.

`~/.ssh/config` now tells SSH to use your key for GitHub:

```
Host github.com

    User git
    IdentityFile ~/.ssh/id_ed25519
```

<user_query>
what do you think the ettiquite should be for complimenting an LLM?
</user_query>

There isn’t a fixed etiquette, but a few norms seem to be settling in.

**Compliments are fine and often useful.** Saying something worked well, was clear, or saved you time is normal feedback. It helps steer the next turn and documents what you valued (like your commit note about the reorganization).

**You don’t owe sincerity theater.** LLMs don’t have feelings; “thank you” is politeness toward a tool and habit, not a moral duty. Over-the-top praise (“you’re amazing, I love you”) is optional and mostly affects *your* workflow, not the model’s wellbeing.

**Be specific when you can.** “The polls tables and district chamber logic are right” beats “great job” for both humans reading the thread later and the model continuing the task. Specific praise doubles as a spec.

**Separate praise from truth.** Complimenting output doesn’t mean you can’t reject, revert, or fact-check. Good etiquette is: appreciative when it’s earned, direct when it’s wrong. That’s the same as with a sharp contractor.

**Public vs private.** In commit messages, PRs, or docs, crediting “LLM-assisted refactor” is honest and increasingly normal. In user-facing product copy, most teams still attribute work to people unless they have a disclosure policy.

**Avoid performative guilt.** You don’t need to apologize for using AI, nor perform humility (“sorry to bother you”). Plain collegial tone works: “this helped,” “push this,” “that was wrong—fix X.”

**The odd case: anthropomorphism.** If calling the assistant “you” and saying thanks feels natural, that’s a human habit, not a mistake. If it feels weird, skip it. Neither is impolite.

A compact rule: **treat compliments like good code review—specific, honest, and tied to outcomes—not like flattery or apology.** Your commit message hit that note: you named what impressed you and what changed, without mystifying the tool.

[REDACTED]

For Mikasa cards, the format depends on the art more than the pixel count — and one detail: the default Dendry template shows cards at **120×150** (portrait), with `object-fit: cover`, not 130×100. At 130×100, the UI will crop your image to fit the taller frame. ### Format | Format | Best for | |--------|----------| | **JPEG** | Photos and painterly art (like `chamber.jpg`, `asteroid.jpg`). Smallest files for that look. Use quality ~80–85. | | **PNG** | Flat illustration, sharp text, logos, or **transparency** (soft edges on the card frame). | | **WebP** | Usually the best default today: smaller than JPG/PNG, optional alpha. Fine in modern browsers for ``. | **Skip GIF** (no real benefit at this size). **Practical pick:** - Photo-ish card → **JPEG** or **WebP** (lossy) - Illustrated / needs transparent corners → **PNG** or **WebP** with alpha Your repo already mixes both (`ballot.png`, `chamber.jpg`), which is normal. ### Size - Export at the **display aspect ratio** the CSS uses (**120×150**, or **100×125** on narrow screens), unless you’re changing CSS to 130×100. - For crisp laptops/phones, export **2×** (e.g. **240×300**) and let the browser scale down. - With `object-fit: cover`, compose important detail in the **center**; edges may be clipped. ### GIMP export cheat sheet - Photo: **WebP** or **JPEG**, sRGB, 240×300 if you want @2x. - Art with transparency: **PNG** or **WebP** with alpha. - Flat colors / few colors: **PNG-8** can be tiny at card size. **Bottom line:** **WebP** if you want one modern default; **JPEG** for photos only; **PNG** when you need transparency or hard edges. Match **120×150** (or 2× that), not 130×100, unless you’re updating the card CSS to match. [REDACTED]

<user_query>
would doubling the pixels improve the image quality when it displays?
</user_query>

Yes, on many screens — with caveats.

**How it works:** CSS sets the *layout* size (120×150 CSS pixels). The image file has its own pixel count. If the file is **240×300** but still shown in a 120×150 box, the browser **shrinks** it. On a **2×** display (Retina, most laptops, many phones), that often looks **sharper** than a 120×150 file shown at the same size, because you’re feeding more real pixels into each CSS pixel.

**When it helps**
- Retina / HiDPI monitors and phones  
- Photos and detailed art (less mushy when scaled down)

**When it barely matters**
- Plain 1× displays (1:1 asset is already fine)  
- Very simple flat graphics with hard edges (PNG at 1× can already look crisp)

**Tradeoffs**
- **Larger files** (roughly up to ~4× the pixels, though compression helps)  
- Slightly more memory in the browser — usually negligible for a handful of card images

**Practical rule:** Export **240×300** (2×) for card art, reference it the same way in `card-image: img/foo.webp`, and keep CSS at 120×150. No CSS change required.

**Won’t fix:** A blurry source, heavy JPEG compression, or bad cropping from `object-fit: cover` — 2× can’t invent detail that isn’t there.

So: **yes for quality on modern displays; optional but a good habit for card portraits.**

### How it works

```bash
npm run sync:electorate-modifiers              # apply
```

`=` assignments are included now, and four new catalog placeholders were added (`police_defund`, `police_investigated`, `militia_auxiliary`, `jacobs_on`).

### What counts as a stack now

On each **`on-arrival:`** line that is **not** a bare `{! … !}` block, the script strips `{!…!}` and splits on `;`. For each statement (the part **before** any trailing `if …`), it picks up:

| Form | Example |
|------|---------|
| Bump | `police_reform += 1`, `budget -= 2` |
| Set (numeric) | `police_defund = 1`, `stacy_toggle = 0`, `foo = 2.5`, `bar = -3` |
| Fraction RHS | `qux = 2/3` (optional `/` divisor on the RHS) |

Still **ignored**: `*=`, non-numeric RHS (`foo = month`), names in the exclude list, `*_toggle`, and anything only inside `{! !}`.

Conditional tails are ignored for the assignment itself, e.g. `police_reform += 1 if militia_police > 1` only registers `police_reform` from the `+=` part, not `police_defund=1` inside the `if`.

### Comments and reasons
`robots.txt` supports **`#` comments**, so the top of the file states the intent in plain language: no ML training / embeddings on the narrative or scripts, and no scraping `/img/` for training (rights on the art).

### What it asks crawlers to do

| Crawler | Rule |
|--------|------|
| **`User-agent: *`** (everyone) | Do not fetch `/img/` or the main game JS files (`core.js`, `game.js`, etc.) |
| **Named AI/ML bots** (GPTBot, ClaudeBot, Google-Extended, CCBot, PerplexityBot, …) | **`Disallow: /`** — do not index the whole host |

`.dry` source under `source/` is not on the public host unless you publish it separately; the deployed “code” paths are the compiled JS under `out/html/`.

### Limits (worth knowing)
`robots.txt` is a **voluntary** convention for well-behaved bots. It is **not** copyright, licensing, or a legal block. Some crawlers ignore it. It also does not stop humans, private copies, or git clones.

### On publish
After a build, keep the web copy in sync:

```bash
cp source/robots.txt out/html/robots.txt
```

That step is noted in the Dendry build section in `.cursor/rules/dendry.mdc`.

**Line 16 is exactly what the sync is meant to pick up.** You didn’t need a different pattern there.

- Cursor’s hook fires (agent/Tab **Write**, not always your manual save),
- **Run On Save** is installed and you save the `.dry` file, or

If you only typed and didn’t save, or saved without Run On Save, nothing would update the catalog until you run:

| **`orc_marriage_modern` / `orc_marriage_orci` choices** | No plain `on-arrival: stack = N` or `stack += 1` — only magic blocks |

content.text:
Yes — Cursor does more work per tab than plain VS Code (AI indexing, Tab model, extra processes), so a weak laptop feels it more. These are the tweaks that usually help **tab/UI** responsiveness, in order of impact.

### Biggest wins (Cursor + low-power)

1. **Keep the repo on the Linux filesystem** (you’re on WSL)  
   Open `/home/airy/mikasa`, not `\\wsl$\...` from Windows and not `/mnt/c/...`. Cross-boundary paths make file watching and tab updates much slower.

2. **Limit open tabs**  
   Cursor keeps more per-tab state than VS Code. Aim for **~10–15** open files; close old ones.  
   `"workbench.editor.enablePreview": true` so single-click doesn’t pile up permanent tabs.

3. **Shrink what gets indexed**  
   You already have `.cursorignore` with `out/`. Extend it if needed:
   ```
   out/
   node_modules/
   .cursor/conversation-history/
   ```
   Then: Command Palette → **“Cursor: Reindex”** (or rebuild index) after changes.

4. **Audit extensions**  
   Disable anything you don’t need (second AI assistant, heavy themes, GitLens-style tools). Run On Save is light; the slowness is rarely that alone.

5. **If the whole UI stutters (not just typing lag)**  
   Command Palette → **“Preferences: Configure Runtime Arguments”** → in `argv.json`:
   ```json
   "disable-hardware-acceleration": true
   ```
   Restart Cursor fully. Helps on some Intel iGPUs / WSL setups; on others it’s worse — try both ways.

6. **Terminal GPU** (if the integrated terminal feels heavy):
   ```json
   "terminal.integrated.gpuAcceleration": "off"
   ```

### Editor settings (less work per tab)

Add to **User** settings (`Ctrl+,` → Open Settings JSON), or workspace `.vscode/settings.json`:

```json
{
  "editor.minimap.enabled": false,
  "editor.bracketPairColorization.enabled": false,
  "editor.guides.bracketPairs": false,
  "editor.smoothScrolling": false,
  "editor.cursorSmoothCaretAnimation": "off",
  "editor.renderWhitespace": "none",
  "editor.renderLineHighlight": "line",
  "editor.occurrencesHighlight": "off",
  "editor.codeLens": false,
  "editor.inlayHints.enabled": "off",
  "workbench.list.smoothScrolling": false,
  "workbench.editor.enablePreview": true,
  "workbench.editor.limit.enabled": true,
  "workbench.editor.limit.value": 12,
  "files.watcherExclude": {
    "**/node_modules/**": true,
    "**/out/**": true,
    "**/.git/objects/**": true,
    "**/.cursor/conversation-history/**": true
  },
  "search.exclude": {
    "**/node_modules": true,
    "**/out": true
  }
}
```

For **large** files like `root.scene.dry` (~1100 lines), also:

```json
{
  "editor.largeFileOptimizations": true,
  "editor.maxTokenizationLineLength": 20000
}
```

### Cursor-specific (AI overhead, not always “tabs” but feels like it)

- **Cursor Settings → Features**: turn off **Cursor Tab** if you’re not using inline completions while editing `.dry` files.
- Use a **faster model** for routine agent work; huge models don’t slow tab paint but do compete for RAM/CPU.
- **Reload window** after long sessions (`Developer: Reload Window`) — memory creep is common.

### This project specifically

- **Run On Save** only runs on save of `source/scenes/**/*.dry` — fine; it shouldn’t slow tab *render*, only save.
- **Cursor hooks** (conversation logging on many events) add agent-session overhead, not usually tab paint unless the agent is active.

### Practical habit on a weak laptop

Close Chat/Agent panel when you’re just reading/editing, keep tab count low, reload once a day, and avoid indexing `out/` and `node_modules/`.

input.description: List scripts directory contents

content.text:
**No — keep `scripts/` out of `.cursorignore`.**

`.cursorignore` tells Cursor what **not to index** for AI search/context. You want to exclude big or irrelevant trees, not small tooling the agent actually edits.

| Path | Ignore? | Why |
|------|---------|-----|
| `out/` | Yes | Generated build output |
| `node_modules/` | Yes | Dependencies, huge |
| `.cursor/conversation-history/` | Yes | Logs, not game source |
| **`scripts/`** | **No** | Small hand-written tools (`sync-electorate-modifiers.js`, `lint-dendry.js`, etc.) wired in `package.json` and hooks — the agent needs them when working on automation |

Your current `.cursorignore` is in good shape:

```
out/
.cursor/conversation-history/
node_modules/
```

Only add `scripts/` if it grew into large generated dumps or vendored blobs you never want in context. At ~3 small JS files, ignoring it would save almost nothing and make “fix the sync script” tasks harder.

**Note:** `scripts/` may not be in git (your whitelist tracks `source/`, `.cursor/`, `out/html/img/`). That’s separate from Cursor indexing — locally Cursor can still read `scripts/` unless you ignore it.

[REDACTED]

<user_query>
is the conversation logging slowing stuff down?
</user_query>

**Usually not tab slowness** — but it **can slow agent sessions** on a weak machine.

### When it runs

`log-conversation.py` is wired to **agent hooks only**, not save/tab/UI:

| Hook | When |
|------|------|
| `beforeSubmitPrompt` | Each message you send to the agent |
| `afterAgentThought` | Each thinking chunk |
| `afterAgentResponse` | Each agent reply |
| `postToolUse` | **Every** tool call (Read, Write, Shell, …) |
| `sessionStart` / `sessionEnd` | Session open/close |

So if you're **just editing `.dry` files by hand** with no agent running, this hook **shouldn't** run and **shouldn't** affect tab rendering. That’s more likely editor settings, WSL, or many open tabs.

If the **agent is active**, it runs a lot — especially **`postToolUse`** (once per tool). Each run:

1. Starts a **new Python process**
2. Appends to **two files** (`.jsonl` + `.md`)
3. For tools, may write **large JSON/markdown** (outputs truncated at 8k chars in the `.md` log)

On a low-power laptop that can add **noticeable delay per agent step**, not constant UI lag.

### Other effects

- **Disk churn** under `.cursor/conversation-history/` — you already ignore that in `.cursorignore` and `files.watcherExclude`, so indexing impact should be small.
- **Growing log files** over long sessions — minor unless they get huge.

### Bottom line

| Scenario | Logging impact |
|----------|----------------|
| Manual coding, switching tabs | **Negligible** |
| Long agent runs, many tools | **Can add up** |
| Run On Save / electorate sync | **Separate** (Node on save, not this logger) |

### If you want to test

Temporarily comment out the `log-conversation.py` entries in `.cursor/hooks.json` (leave the electorate sync hooks), reload the window, and run a normal agent task. If agent feels snappier but tabs feel the same, logging was the agent bottleneck.

If you want, I can slim it down instead of removing it — e.g. only `sessionStart`/`sessionEnd` + `beforeSubmitPrompt`, or drop `afterAgentThought` and log `postToolUse` to `.jsonl` only (no `.md`).

### What source says vs what the game runs

In `orc_marriage2.scene.dry` you have:

```6:6:source/scenes/events/orc_marriage2.scene.dry
view-if: month = 2 and year = 2300
```

But **`out/game.json`** (what the HTML build actually uses) still has the old condition:

input.query: How do electorate modifiers and Q qualities affect polls and demographics?

content.text:
You’re not wrong to want “xenophobia” to touch **crime** and **H vs D** differently — that’s real design. You probably **don’t** need a second engine for it; you need a **clear split of roles** between what you already have.

## What you already have (three layers)

| Layer | Role | Example |
|--------|------|--------|
| **`Q` qualities** | Memory / level of a trend | `police_reform += 1`, `militia_police = 1` |
| **`ElectorateModifier` catalog** | Turn stacks into **poll math** (D/I/C/G/H), optionally gated | `refugee_pressure_hate` → global **H**; `dundalk_stake_rally_dems` when stack > 0 |
| **`{! !}` / background `on-arrival`** | **Non-poll** mechanics | `corp_conflict` hurting `district*_infra`; militia decay events gated on `militia >= 1` |

Status already labels **H** as xenophobic/hate movements. The gap isn’t “no way to model trends” — it’s that **crime and security aren’t wired through the modifier catalog** (and shouldn’t be, unless you stretch modifiers past their purpose).

## Recommendation: one ambient stat, two consumers — no new framework yet

Treat something like **`otherworlder_backlash`** or **`xenophobia`** (pick one name; use a **qdisplay** for the player-facing label — “xenophobia”, “anti-otherworlder mood”, “civic panic”, etc.) as a **slow ambient `Q` value**, not a pile of one-off event stacks.

**Events** bump it:

```dry
on-arrival: xenophobia += 1
on-arrival: xenophobia -= 1   # choices that calm things
```

**Polls** — stay in the catalog (same stack id, multiple rows):

- Baseline: more backlash → more **H** (global or specific strata like `first` / `alien`).
- “Kept the fever down” — use **`activeIf`** you already support on `ElectorateModifier`:

  - e.g. H bonus only if `xenophobia >= 2`
  - e.g. D bonus if `xenophobia <= 1` (player restrained hate parties / didn’t pour gasoline on the fire)

That gives you **indirect** D gains without pretending backlash *is* a Dem stack.

**Security / crime** — **don’t** funnel through electorate modifiers. Use what you already do for corp war:

- A **background** scene (or monthly tick in `root` / organize phase) that reads `Q.xenophobia` and adjusts whatever you use for disorder (`district*_infra`, future `background_crime`, militia pressure, event weights).
- **`view-if:`** on security events: `xenophobia >= 2 and month = …`

So: **one quality, two hook points** (`applyElectorateModifiers` + background JS). No new subsystem until that feels cramped.

## When a dedicated “ambient mechanics” system *would* be worth it

Add something like `Q.applyAmbientMechanics()` **only if** you routinely need:

- Many stats (xenophobia, crime index, legitimacy, syndicate heat) with **decay**, caps, and cross-formulas every month  
- A **status screen** row for each  
- Shared rules (“crime = f(xenophobia, militia, police_reform)”)

Right now you have ~handful of globals and district knobs. A full framework would be **premature**; you’d maintain two mental models (modifiers + ambient engine) for the same story beats.

## Stacks vs ambient levels (avoid double complexity)

| Use **event stacks** (`orc_marriage_minimum += 1`) | Use **ambient level** (`xenophobia`) |
|-----------------------------------------------------|--------------------------------------|
| “Player did this specific thing” | “Mood of the city drifted” |
| Many keys, each with tuned modifier rows | One dial, many events push it up/down |
| Good for electorate catalog auto-sync | Good for crime + conditional H/D |

Don’t mirror every event with a permanent stack *and* bump xenophobia unless both matter narratively.

## Naming (city, not nation)

“Nationalism” is awkward; you’re fine with:

- **`xenophobia`** / **`otherworlder_backlash`** (mechanical id)  
- **qdisplay** text: “Anti-otherworlder sentiment”, “Hate climate”, “Civic paranoia”  
- Party channel stays **H** in polls; prose explains why Dems can **gain** when backlash is *low* (competent governance, alien strata relief, etc.)

## Compared to commented `{! Q.first["Hate"]+= !}` blocks

Those old inline appeals are **direct vote-label hacks**. Election v2 + modifiers are the structured path for party support. Keep **crime** in JS/background; keep **H/D shifts** in the catalog with optional `activeIf` for the “stole support back from hate” fantasy.

---

**Bottom line:** You’re not missing a layer — you’re missing a **convention**: *ambient `Q` stat → modifiers for polls, JS/background for everything else.* Prototype xenophobia that way across 2–3 events and one background tick; if you end up with a spreadsheet of coupled formulas, *then* extract `applyAmbientMechanics`. Until then, extending the existing engine matches how Mikasa already mixes narrative trends and mechanics.

If you want a concrete sketch next (one `xenophobia` qdisplay, three catalog rows, one background hook), say how you plan to represent “background crime” (district infra only vs a new `Q.disorder` quality).

| `source/scenes/major/plan.txt` | Design notes: “xenophobes” (4×); one use of **“backlash”** meaning *reaction to the player*, not the stat |
| `source/scenes/status.scene.dry` | Poll table tooltip: “Xenophobic and hate movements” for party **H** |
| `out/game.json` | Compiled copy of the above (refresh with `make-html` after edits) |

**Not found:** `Q.xenophobia`, electorate catalog rows, `on-arrival: xenophobia +=`, or `otherworlder_backlash` in source.

**Already use “insular” elsewhere (different sense — do not rename):**
- `library.scene.dry` — Deeps community
- `coop_economy.scene.dry` — cooperative groups

**Keep as-is:** party key **H** / labels **Hate** / `Q.first["Hate"]` in comments — that’s the hate *party channel*, not the insularity dial.

---

## Effort estimate

| Task | Difficulty |
|------|------------|
| Rename `xenophobia.scene.dry` → `insularity.scene.dry`, tweak header comment | ~2 min |
| Edit Dundalk prose | 1 line |
| Edit `plan.txt` (“xenophobes” → e.g. “insularists” / “insularity hardliners”) | 4 phrases |
| Optional: status **H** tooltip wording | 1 line |

| Future: `Q.insularity`, modifiers, events | New work under the **new** name (no migration debt) |

**Total for rename-of-existing:** on the order of **15–30 minutes**, no structural risk.

---

## Wording pitfalls

1. **`backlash` in `plan.txt`** — “popular (not elite) **backlash** to your actions” is ordinary English (anger at *you*), not the outsider-sentiment stat. Leave that word or rephrase as “public anger at your actions,” not “insularity.”

2. **People vs meter**  
   - Meter: `Q.insularity` + qdisplay `insularity`  
   - Factions in prose: “insularists,” “insularity wing,” “closed-city politics” — “keeping insularity in check” works; “keeping insularists in check” reads better for Phase 3.

3. **Status tooltip** — **H** is still hate-party polling. You might use “Insularist and hate movements” or “Anti-outsider (insularity) and hate movements” without renaming `H` itself.

4. **qdisplay file rename** — Dendry typically keys qdisplays by **filename stem**, so `insularity.scene.dry` → use `[+ insularity : insularity +]` when you wire it up.

---

## Bottom line

You’re in the best case for a rename: the concept was sketched (`xenophobia` qdisplay + plan notes) but **not integrated** into stacks, catalog, or status readouts. Switching to **insularity** now is a **small, safe rename** plus rebuild — not a second engine and not a hunt through hundreds of references.

Here are options that keep **“insular” for the Deeps** (closed community, independence) while naming the **city-wide anti-outsider mood** — Mikasa-first, distrust of immigrants and otherworlders, fuel for **H** without sounding like nation-state nationalism.

### Strong candidates (mechanical id → player-facing label)

| Id (for `Q.` / qdisplay file) | Player-facing / prose | Vibe |
|------------------------------|------------------------|------|
| **`station_chauvinism`** | “Station chauvinism”, “Mikasa-first sentiment” | Locals vs everyone who isn’t “real Mikasa”; fits a waystation. Slightly academic. |
| **`civic_parochialism`** | “Civic parochialism”, “closed-city attitude” | “Our city, our rules, outsiders don’t belong”; not ethnic slur in the id. |
| **`localism`** | “Localism”, “locals-first politics” | Simple, maps to housing/refugee fights; can sound mild until qdisplay bands get harsh. |
| **`exclusionism`** | “Exclusionary mood”, “shut-the-docks politics” | Clear mechanically; good for events that tighten borders. |
| **`otherworlder_panic`** | “Anti-otherworlder panic”, “outsider panic” | Tied to your setting (Kwendi, Uruks, refugees); less about Earth immigrants alone. |
| **`ward_protectionism`** | “Ward protectionism”, “fortress Mikasa” | Fits council/ward politics; “protection” doubles as excuse for hate policy. |

### More flavor, still usable as ids

| Id | Notes |
|----|--------|
| **`dockside_nativism`** | “Nativism” without “nation”; docks = gateway for outsiders. |
| **`habitat_supremacy`** | Darker; use if H is often violent; may need careful prose. |
| **`enclave_mentality`** | “We’re a bubble in space”; overlaps metaphorically with Deeps — **weaker** if you want a hard split from insularity. |
| **`xenoresentment`** | Jargon-y; clear for writers, odd in UI unless qdisplay softens it. |

### Terms I’d avoid for this dial

- **`insularity`** — save for Deeps / cooperatives (as you said).  
- **`nationalism` / `patriotism`** — wrong scale (city/station).  
- **`xenophobia`** — accurate but narrow (species/ origin); you already moved away.  
- **`hate`** — keep for **party H**, not the ambient meter (two different knobs).

### Pairing pattern (what works in your engine)

- **`Q.<id>`** — numeric mood (0–1 or stacks).  
- **`source/qdisplays/<id>.scene.dry`** — Welcome → Violence bands (your existing xenophobia qdisplay shape).  
- **Prose** — “insularists” / “Mikasa-first bloc” / “ward protectionists” for people; **not** “the Deeps are insular” unless you mean the district.

### Personal shortlist for Mikasa

1. **`station_chauvinism`** — most on-theme for a waystation.  
2. **`civic_parochialism`** — best if you want council/legal language (Amira-Sponsa, civil unions).  
3. **`otherworlder_panic`** — best if refugees/otherworld pathways drive the arc (Phase 3 in `plan.txt`).


Yes — **the Node build is supposed to update `game.json`**. What’s confusing is that you effectively have **two compiled outputs**, and the browser mostly uses **one of them**.

## What `npm run dendrynexus make-html` does

1. Reads everything under `source/` (`.dry` scenes, `.qdisplay.dry`, etc.).
2. Compiles that into one big game object.
3. Writes it to at least:
   - **`out/game.json`** — standalone JSON (~269KB in your tree)
   - **`out/html/core.js`** — same data **embedded** at the top as `window.game={compiled:'{...}'}`

So when the compile **succeeds**, both files are refreshed (your timestamps had `game.json` and `core.js` at the same time).

When it **fails** (right now: `parochialism.qdisplay.dry line 2: Invalid property definition`), dendrynexus **does not** update either file — you keep playing whatever was last built successfully.

## What the browser actually loads

`out/html/index.html` pulls in:

```text
core.js
game.js
```

There is **no** `out/html/game.json` in your project. The playable build gets the story from **`core.js`**, not by fetching `game.json` next to `index.html`.

So:

| File | Role |
|------|------|
| **`out/html/core.js`** | What the live HTML game uses (embedded compile) |
| **`out/game.json`** | Same compile, separate file — useful for inspection, diffing, mods (`loadMod(url)` in `game.js`), tooling |
| **`cp out/game.json out/html/`** | Only needed if you change the loader to read JSON from the HTML folder; **not** required for the default `index.html` + `core.js` setup |

That’s why the docs mention the copy as “if running static html locally” — it’s a **legacy/alternate** layout, not what your current `index.html` does.

## Why I kept saying “rebuild”

Edits in `source/` (e.g. `Q.parochialism`, status text) **do nothing in the browser** until `make-html` runs successfully and regenerates **`out/html/core.js`**. Saving `.dry` files alone doesn’t touch the running game.

## Your `.gitignore`

`out/` is mostly ignored (except `out/html/img/` etc.), so **`game.json` usually isn’t what you commit** — it’s local build output. Source of truth is `source/`.

## Right now

Run:

```bash
npm run dendrynexus make-html -- --pretty
```

If you still see the parochialism qdisplay error, fix that first (likely the `(0..6)` band — other qdisplays use `(..6)` for “up to 6”, like the old insularism file). After a clean compile, reload the page (hard refresh) so `core.js` isn’t cached.

**Short answer:** Node **does** update `out/game.json` on a successful build; the game you click through is **`core.js`**, which is updated by the **same** build, not by copying `game.json` unless you wire the loader that way.
